title: A heckler on opening night in Berlin recalling the Senegalese
summary: After the first show at the Admiral's Palace, a drunk German objected to black performers, and a dancer's punch sent him off.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Now, you've told us about some of the happy experiences during your tour in Europe. Did you ever run into any more unfortunate experiences while in Europe?

I remember distinctly the opening night after the show -- the opening performance in Berlin in Admiral's Palace -- that was on Frederickstrasse -- there were people out front crowded around the performers and musicians and we were receiving the congratulations from the public who had seen our first show -- how great -- they loved the music and all --
What year was this, Mr. Bushell?

1925, May 3 or 6th, something like that. And everybody was commenting and saying how well we performed, how much they loved our work, and saying what a great show it was. But one German evidently had too many drinks and he came right up into the crowd and tore open his shirt and said, 'I'm a German to my heart. I don't understand why the government allows these black people to come to our country. During the war they cut off our noses, they cut off our ears,' he's speaking about the Senegalese, you know. The Senegalese didn't take prisoners, they just -- when a German went down they just cut off the end of his nose or an ear and put it on a string. That way when he went back home that shows how many men he captured -- killed rather. He said, 'They did that to us and I have not forgotten. And I am not going to stand for it. They should run them out of Germany.'
He was speaking in German. I understand, I studied German from a kid -- my grandfather was German, so I

studied German in school. And he turned around to one of the dancers, Rufus Green to be exact, and grabbed Green by the coat. When he grabbed Green he clipped him on the chin and down he went. Now, he was so drunk he couldn't stand up. When Green hit him he went down and got up and shook himself and walked just as straight down Frederickstrasse as you've ever seen anybody right out of the crowd. That straightened him out. We found out in those days, you know, the Germans used to carry large canes. And a German is funny. If he hollers at you and you wilt, he'll beat you to death. But if he hollers at you and you holler back and get up in his face, he's ready to go. We found that out. We found the weak spot. I'll tell you what we found. We were sitting in a backroom in a place called the Domstatterhof one night. There were five of us in there having beer, and six or seven Heidelberg students came in. You could tell Heidelberg students because they were medical students and they all had scars on the left side of their face. They're from medical school, I think it was Heidelberg -- but they all had scars on the left side -- they were all dueling students, you know. Everybody's got a cut -- all the medical - old Germans have cuts on the side of their face from school. They locked the door saying, "Now, we're going to run the schwartzes out tonight.
